```cs
public static async Task DeleteCategoryAsync(ShopDb db, ICacheManager cache, IMethodCacheKeys keys, int categoryId,
    CancellationToken ct)
{
    // Without a transaction the delete is committed when it returns: invalidate at once
    await db.Products.Where(p => p.CategoryId == categoryId).ExecuteDeleteAsync(ct);
    await cache.InvalidateTagAsync(
        keys.Tag<IProductReads>(r => r.ListAsync(categoryId), "category:{categoryId}"), CancellationToken.None);
}
```

`InvalidateAfterCommit` takes tags exactly as cached methods write them. Build them with `IMethodCacheKeys.Tag`, or
with `MethodCacheKeys.Part` around each value; [MC0024](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0024) reports a hand-built tag
that formats a value differently. Outside a transaction, queued tags wait for the next commit, a successful
`SaveChanges` or a transaction's `Commit`, and are invalidated when the context is disposed if none comes. A rollback
doesn't drop them, since they don't belong to it.

Writes outside EF Core, such as Dapper or another service, are covered in
[When the write happens somewhere else](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/invalidation.md#when-the-write-happens-somewhere-else).

## Document databases

Azure Cosmos DB and MongoDB have EF Core providers. Entity tags and `InvalidateAfterCommit` work with them, since
both act on `SaveChanges`. Cosmos DB has no transactions you begin yourself in EF Core, so each `SaveChanges` is the
commit. A MongoDB transaction you begin with `BeginTransaction` isn't seen by the package; its tags are invalidated
at the context's next save after the commit, or when the context is disposed.

With these providers, a context can't tell which rows it loaded until its first save. A changed row it loaded before
then is read once when it is saved, as a row changed without loading is, if its tags use more than its key.

## Testing

Use SQLite in memory, or your real database, with the same registration. A test that writes to the database without
EF Core needs its own invalidation ([Testing](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/testing.md#when-a-test-writes-to-the-database-directly)).


---

<!-- source: docs/features/fail-safe.md -->

# Fail-safe

Fail-safe keeps an expired value for a while and returns it when calling the method again fails, so a database or API
outage shows slightly old data instead of errors. It is off by default.

Chapter 8 of the [console demo](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/samples/MethodCache.Demo) shows a failing API, retry suppression,
recovery and a slow response that finishes after the caller receives its fallback. A fake clock controls the
expiry, retry and timeout windows; the same scenario runs in the docs tests.

## Turning it on

For every cached method at once:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(config => config.Defaults(o => o
    .WithFailSafe(TimeSpan.FromHours(1))                    // how long an expired value is kept as a fallback
    .WithFailSafeTimeout(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200))    // optional: don't wait longer than this when a fallback exists
    .WithFailSafeRetryAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))));    // optional: reuse the fallback this long before trying again
```

or in `appsettings.json`:

```json
{
  "MethodCache": {
    "FailSafe": { "Duration": "01:00:00", "Timeout": "00:00:00.200", "RetryAfter": "00:00:30" }
  }
}
```

## What happens

- **When the method throws**, the caller gets the expired value if it is younger than the fail-safe duration. That
  value is then reused for the retry delay (`RetryAfter`, default 30 seconds) before the method is called again, so a
  failing dependency isn't hammered; no [refresh-ahead](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/expiration.md#refresh-ahead) reload starts during that time
  either.
- **When the method is slow** and a `Timeout` is set, the caller gets the expired value after it and the call
  finishes in the background; its result replaces the old value. Without an expired value the caller waits as usual.
  Because the call may outlive the request, a scoped or transient service makes it on a new instance from a new DI
  scope, disposed when the call ends, whenever a fallback exists and a `Timeout` is set (the instance has none of the
  request's own state, such as values set on the instance). The caller's `HttpContext` and `AsyncLocal` values still
  flow to it, as it starts on the caller's call. Singletons use their one instance.
- A caller's own cancellation is never treated as a failure, so it doesn't trigger fail-safe.
- A value that was invalidated (its key, a tag or a clear) or replaced is never a fallback, also when that happened
  while the reload ran: callers then wait for the reload, or get its exception.
- Without an expired value, the exception reaches the caller as usual.
- `GetOrCreateManyAsync` works the same way for each key: when the batch factory throws, each key gets its own
  fallback, and the exception is thrown only when a key has none.

## Per method

A method or group can change any of it, and its own setting wins over the central one. `[Cache]` takes the same three
settings as `FailSafe`, `FailSafeTimeout` and `FailSafeRetryAfter`:

```cs
public interface IAccountService
{
    [Cache(Duration = "00:05:00", FailSafe = "01:00:00", FailSafeTimeout = "00:00:00.200")]
    Task<Rates> GetRatesAsync();

    [Cache(FailSafe = "off")]   // a balance must never be old, so an error is better
    Task<decimal> GetBalanceAsync(int accountId);
}
```

In code, use the builder methods with the same names: `WithFailSafe`, `WithFailSafeTimeout` and
`WithFailSafeRetryAfter`, for example `Configure(o => o.WithFailSafeTimeout(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100)))` to
change only the timeout. `o.WithFailSafe(TimeSpan.Zero)` turns fail-safe off. In `appsettings.json`, a method takes
`FailSafe` (a time span or `"off"`), `FailSafeTimeout` and `FailSafeRetryAfter`.

## Limits

> [!NOTE]
> The fallback lives in each instance's memory, so right after a restart there is none until the method has succeeded
> once.

Cancelling a call stops its wait for the distributed cache, a slow method or a fail-safe value. Work that other callers share may finish for them, and a cancelled call doesn't count as a failure.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/conditional-caching.md -->

# Conditional caching

Sometimes a result should be returned but not remembered: an empty search, a product that doesn't exist yet, a
response that says "try again later".

Chapter 9 of the [console demo](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/samples/MethodCache.Demo) skips missing products and proves that a
newly created product is visible on the next lookup, while existing products are cached.

## CacheWhen

`CacheWhen` stores a result only when the predicate returns true:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(config =>
{
    // Don't remember empty search results: the next search asks the database again
    config.Method((IProductService s) => s.SearchAsync(Any<string>.Value))
          .CacheWhen(results => results.Count > 0);

    // A product that doesn't exist yet may be created any moment
    config.Method((IProductService s) => s.FindAsync(Any<int>.Value))
          .CacheWhen(product => product is not null);
});
```

- A rejected result is still returned to the caller, and the next call runs the method again.
- The entry it would have replaced, including a fail-safe value, stays.
- The predicate runs once per load, and on each value read from the distributed cache: a value it rejects there is
  skipped and the method runs. It never runs on a hit in memory. If it throws, the result is returned and not stored.
- `config.Method(...).CacheWhen` gets the method's result type. A `CacheWhen<T>` set elsewhere for a type the method
  can't return, such as `CacheWhen<string>` on a method that returns `int`, fails where it is set instead of silently
  caching nothing: in code with an `InvalidOperationException` at startup, and in a runtime override with an
  `ArgumentException` that leaves the policy as it was. A generic method's result type depends on the call, so there
  the call throws the `InvalidOperationException`.
- It is set for one method in code only, so it can't come from `appsettings.json`. In `Defaults` or a group it fails
  at startup. `.CacheWhen(...)` and `.Configure(o => o.CacheWhen<T>(...))` set the same thing: the last call wins.
  `Any<T>.Value` stands for any argument.

> [!TIP]
> To stop caching `null` everywhere, set `CacheNullValues = false` on the [memory cache](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/memory-cache.md) instead.

## Skipping the cache for one call

With [manual caching](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/manual-caching.md), `WithEnabled` decides per call whether to use the cache at all:

```cs
var results = await cache.GetOrCreateAsync(
    $"search:{text}",
    async ct => await search(),
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10))
          .WithEnabled(!preview));   // preview requests skip the cache entirely
```

With `WithEnabled(false)`, the factory runs and its result is neither read from nor written to the cache.
To decide from the result instead, use `CacheWhen` ([Validation](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md#validation)).


---

<!-- source: docs/features/configuration.md -->

# Configuration

A cached method's policy (duration, sliding expiration, refresh-ahead, fail-safe, tags, group, version) can come from
four layers. Change it in `appsettings.json` or at runtime, and the next call uses it, without a redeploy.

| Layer | How you set it | Priority | Changes while running |
|-------|----------------|----------|-----------------------|
| Attributes | `[Cache(...)]` on the interface method | 10 (lowest) | No |
| Startup code | `AddMethodCache(config => ...)` | 40 | No |
| Configuration | `AddMethodCache(b => b.FromConfiguration(configuration))` | 50 | Yes, when the configuration reloads |
| Runtime overrides | `IRuntimeCacheConfigurator` | 100 (highest) | Yes |

When several layers configure the same method, they are merged setting by setting, and the highest layer that sets a
setting wins. A runtime override of `Duration` leaves the attribute's `Tags` in place.

Tags are the exception: they are combined, not replaced. Tags from startup code, `appsettings.json`, runtime overrides
and the defaults are added to the `[Cache]` attribute's tags (without duplicates), so a `[CacheInvalidate]` that
lists an attribute tag always reaches the entry. To replace the tags instead, call `ClearTags()` before `AddTags`
(`o => o.ClearTags().AddTags("orders")`), or set `"ClearTags": true` next to `Tags` for a method in
`appsettings.json`. The tags of the lower layers and of the defaults are then dropped, and an entry without them is
no longer removed by a `[CacheInvalidate]` that lists them.

## Defaults and groups

Within the layers, each setting comes from the most specific place that sets it: the method itself, then its group,
then the defaults.

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(config =>
{
    // Every cached method: fills in what the method leaves unset
    config.Defaults(o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(15)));

    // Methods in the "user-data" group: [Cache(Group = "user-data")] or WithGroup("user-data")
    config.Group("user-data", o => o.WithSlidingExpiration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10)));

    // One method
    config.Method((IUserService s) => s.GetProfileAsync(Any<int>.Value))
          .Configure(o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromHours(2)).WithRefreshAhead(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)));
});
```

- `Defaults` applies to every cached method, also ones that only have `[Cache]`. `[Cache(Duration = "00:10:00")]`
  keeps its ten minutes while the defaults fill in what it leaves out.
- A method joins a group with `[Cache(Group = "name")]`, `WithGroup("name")` in code, or `Group` in `appsettings.json`.
  Group names are case-sensitive. A group's defaults come from `config.Group(...)` and from `"Groups"` in
  `appsettings.json`, which wins where both set a value; a method's own settings win over both.
- `CacheWhen` is set for one method only. In `Defaults` or a group it fails at startup
  ([Conditional caching](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/conditional-caching.md)).
- `Any<T>.Value` stands for any argument when you point at a method.

Startup uses `MethodCacheBuilder`: `Defaults`, `Group`, typed `Method` expressions, `Memory`, `Distributed`,
`Telemetry`, `FromConfiguration`, `FromAssemblyOf` and explicit `AutoRegister(lifetime)`. Redis, SQL Server,
PostgreSQL and MessagePack packages add `UseRedis`, `UseSqlServer`, `UsePostgreSql` and `UseMessagePack`; Core provides
`UseJson`. Use one distributed cache: calling more than one of `UseRedis`, `UseSqlServer` and `UsePostgreSql` throws. `Distributed(...)`, `UseMessagePack` or `UseJson`
without a distributed cache logs a warning, since they have nothing to apply to. `builder.Services` is the service
collection, for a package that adds its own `UseXxx` method.
`Method` on a method without `[Cache]` fails at startup, and on a method that returns nothing (`void`, `Task`,
`ValueTask`) throws an `ArgumentException`.
All integration packages require the exact same Core package version; do not override this bound.
CI uses strict restore (NU1608 as an error) to reject direct-version overrides. Configure services before `AddMethodCache`.
Runtime overrides use the same immutable options builder as startup and manual cache calls.

## appsettings.json

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(methodCache => methodCache.FromConfiguration(builder.Configuration));   // the "MethodCache" section
```

```json
{
  "MethodCache": {
    "Defaults": { "Duration": "00:15:00" },
    "FailSafe": { "Duration": "01:00:00" },
    "Groups": {
      "user-data": { "SlidingExpiration": "00:10:00" }
    },
    "Methods": {
      "[MyApp]MyApp.IUserService.GetProfileAsync": {
        "Duration": "01:00:00",
        "SlidingExpiration": "00:10:00",
        "RefreshAhead": "00:05:00",
        "Tags": ["users"],
        "Version": 1,
        "Notes": "Profiles change rarely"
      },
      "[MyApp]MyApp.IAccountService.GetBalanceAsync": { "FailSafe": "off" }
    }
  }
}
```

- Each key under `Methods` is the **method id**: the escaped assembly simple name in brackets, the full interface name, a dot and the method name (for example `[MyApp]MyApp.IUserService.GetProfileAsync`). Assembly versions do not participate. A generic
  interface is written with its type parameters (`[MyApp]MyApp.IRepository<T>.GetAsync`), and an overloaded method adds its
  parameter types (`[MyApp]MyApp.IUserService.FindAsync(int)`). Parameter types other than built-in ones are qualified by
  namespace (`[MyApp]MyApp.IUsers.Find(MyApp.Request)`), so overloads taking `A.Request` and `B.Request` stay separate. Types
  are named as reflection sees them: a tuple is `System.ValueTuple<int, string>` (element names dropped), `nint` is
  `System.IntPtr` and `dynamic` is `object`. Runtime overrides by method id use the same format, and the parameter
  list is also part of the method's cache keys. The admin endpoints list every method id ([Monitoring](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/monitoring.md)),
  and `IMethodCacheKeys.MethodId<T>(s => s.FindAsync(Any<int>.Value))` returns the id of a call ([Cache keys](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/keys.md)).
- Settings: `Duration`, `SlidingExpiration`, `RefreshAhead` and `FailSafe` (each but `Duration` a time span or `"off"`), `FailSafeTimeout`,
  `FailSafeRetryAfter`, `Tags`, `Version`, `Enabled` and `Distributed`. A group under `Groups` and a method under
  `Methods` can also set `ClearTags` (`true` or `false`): `true` makes their `Tags` replace the lower layers' instead of
  adding to them. Only a method can set `Group`, `Metadata` and `Notes`; in `Defaults` or a group they are an error.
  `Metadata` and `Notes` are recorded for diagnostics and never change caching; to put a method in a group, use
  `Group`. Names are case-insensitive; any other name is an error, so a misspelled `"Durration"` is reported
  instead of ignored. The same goes for the section itself: it holds only `Defaults`, `FailSafe`, `Groups` and
  `Methods`. A leftover `Services` section from 1.0.0-rc.1 is reported as an unknown setting.
- Tag templates such as `"order:{orderId}"` are checked against the parameters of every method they reach, as for
  `[Cache]` ([MC0010](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0010)): a template that names a parameter a method doesn't have
  fails at startup.
- Durations are written as in attributes: `"30s"`, `"5m"`, `"1.5h"`, `"7d"` or `"hh:mm:ss"` (including
  `"d.hh:mm:ss"`); see [Writing a duration](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/expiration.md#writing-a-duration). A bare number such as `"300"` is rejected
  rather than interpreted as days. `Tags` is a list (`["users"]`), and a method's `FailSafe` is one time span: the
  `{ "Duration", "Timeout", "RetryAfter" }` block exists only at the top of the section. Setting the same value in
  that block and in `Defaults` (for example `FailSafe.Timeout` and `Defaults.FailSafeTimeout`) is an error.
- A method can also be listed under an index with a `MethodId` property. Environment variable names can't hold `.`,
  `(` or `<`, so this is how environment variables, Kubernetes `env` or Linux App Service configure a method:

  ```bash
  MethodCache__Methods__0__MethodId="[MyApp]MyApp.IUserService.FindAsync(int)"
  MethodCache__Methods__0__Duration="00:02:00"
  ```

  A method can be listed once. Listing it both by name and under an index, for example by name in
  `appsettings.json` and under an index in an environment variable, fails at startup and names both paths. To
  override one file's settings from another source, list the method under the same index in both.
- `Defaults` applies to every cached method; the top-level `FailSafe` section is described in [Fail-safe](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/fail-safe.md).
- Pass a section name as the second argument to read another section. Environment files such as
  `appsettings.Production.json` work as usual. The section is read when the host starts, so configuration sources
  added after `FromConfiguration`, such as a later `AddJsonFile` or a `WebApplicationFactory`'s test
  settings, apply from the first call.
- Changes apply while the application runs, as soon as the configuration reloads (`appsettings.json` reloads on save
  by default).
- Only methods with `[Cache]` (or listed in `[assembly: CacheInterface]`) have a decorator, so the file can change
  their policy but can't make other methods cached. A method id that matches no cached method, such as a misspelled
  name or an id without its `[Assembly]` prefix, fails at startup and suggests the closest cached id. `*` and
  `group:<name>` are not method ids; use `Defaults` and `Groups`.
- An invalid value, such as a `Duration` that isn't a positive time span, makes the host fail to start with an
  `InvalidOperationException` naming the setting (without a generic host, the first cached call throws). If a
  reloaded file has one, the reload is logged as an error naming the setting's path, never its value, and the
  previous policies stay.

## Runtime overrides

A runtime override of a method wins over that method's other layers (its attribute, startup code and
`appsettings.json`). Use them to change a policy without a deploy, for example to shorten a duration during an
incident:

```cs
var configurator = app.Services.GetRequiredService<IRuntimeCacheConfigurator>();

// One method, strongly typed, with who and why for the audit trail
await configurator.UpsertAsync<IOrdersService>(
    s => s.GetAsync(Any<int>.Value),
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2)),
    new RuntimeOverrideMetadata { Owner = "ops", Reason = "Incident 4211", ExpiresAt = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddHours(4) });

// By method id, for example from an admin form
await configurator.UpsertAsync($"[{typeof(IUserService).Assembly.GetName().Name}]Docs.Configuration.IUserService.GetProfileAsync",
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10)));

// Back to the lower layers
await configurator.RemoveAsync<IOrdersService>(s => s.GetAsync(Any<int>.Value));
await configurator.ClearAsync();
```

| Method | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `UpsertAsync` | Adds or replaces the override for one method, by expression (`UpsertAsync<IOrdersService>(s => s.GetAsync(0), ...)`) or method id |
| `RemoveAsync` / `ClearAsync` | Removes one override, or all of them |
| `GetOverrides()` | Returns the active overrides, ordered by method id, with their options and audit metadata |

The async operations return `ValueTask` and take cancellation last. A method id or expression that reaches no cached
method, or a method that returns nothing, throws an `ArgumentException` naming the closest cached id before
anything is stored. A tag template that doesn't fit the method throws too.
- Overrides change one method each. Group and global defaults come from startup code or `appsettings.json`.
- Tags from an override are added to the method's tags unless the override calls `ClearTags()`.
  `WithEnabled(false)` turns caching off for the method; `WithDistributed(false)` keeps it in memory only.
- An override that changes how the method caches drops the entries cached under the old settings at once; calls
  already running may still return their earlier result. An override that only changes its audit metadata keeps them.
- Overrides live in this instance's memory: they are lost on restart and don't reach other instances. While an override
  changes how a method caches, that method's entries in the distributed cache are this instance's own; removing the
  override invalidates the method and shares entries again
  ([Distributed cache reference](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/reference/distributed.md#policies-and-shared-entries)).
- `RuntimeOverrideMetadata` keeps owner, reason and ticket for the audit trail, and `ExpiresAt` removes the override
  when it passes.
- A changed `appsettings.json` applies on this instance before the reload notification returns. Each instance reloads
  its own configuration; MethodCache doesn't distribute files.

## Seeing the effective policy

`ICacheAdministrator.GetMethods()` shows each method's effective options, where each setting comes from, and whether
its distributed cache entries are shared with other instances or its own because of a runtime override:

```cs
var diagnostics = app.Services.GetRequiredService<ICacheAdministrator>();

foreach (var report in diagnostics.GetMethods())
{
    var sources = string.Join(", ", report.SettingSources.Values.Distinct());
    Console.WriteLine($"{report.MethodId}: Duration={report.Options.Duration}, from {sources}");
}
```

`SettingSources` is keyed by the `CacheEntryOptions` property name (`Duration`, `Tags`, `SlidingExpiration`,
`RefreshAhead`, `Version`, `FailSafe`, `FailSafeTimeout`, `FailSafeRetryAfter`, `Enabled`, `Distributed`), and each
value is a `CacheSettingSource`: `Attribute`, `Code`, `Configuration` or `RuntimeOverride`. A setting no layer sets
is left out. The admin endpoint `GET /methodcache/methods` shows the same, with the sources as strings
([Monitoring](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/monitoring.md)).

## Validation

| Setting | Rule | Checked |
|---------|------|---------|
| `Duration` | A positive time span, and with the built-in memory cache at most `MethodCacheMemoryOptions.MaxExpiration` (7 days by default) | `[Cache]`: at build time ([MC0004](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0004)). Code: `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. JSON: at startup. Longer than `MaxExpiration`: at startup from `[Cache]`, code and JSON, an `ArgumentException` from a runtime override, and an `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` from a manual call |
| `SlidingExpiration`, `RefreshAhead`, `FailSafe` | A positive time span or `"off"`; in code, `TimeSpan.Zero` turns it off | `[Cache]`: at build time ([MC0004](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0004)). Code: `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for a negative value. JSON: at startup |
| `RefreshAhead` | Shorter than `Duration` and `SlidingExpiration` | `[Cache]`: at build time ([MC0023](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0023)). Code: `InvalidOperationException` when the options are built. JSON: at startup |
| `FailSafeTimeout`, `FailSafeRetryAfter` | A positive time span | `[Cache]`: at build time. Code (`WithFailSafeTimeout`, `WithFailSafeRetryAfter`): `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. JSON: at startup |
| `Tags` | Not empty or whitespace; templates name parameters of the method | `[Cache]`: at build time. Code: `AddTags` throws an `ArgumentException` for an empty tag; templates at startup. JSON: at startup |
| `Version` | Zero or more | Code: `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. JSON: at startup. On `[Cache]`, a negative explicit value is MC0021; omission inherits |

`CacheEntryOptions.Builder` applies to startup, configuration, runtime overrides and manual calls. Each setting has one
`With` method named like the attribute setting, such as `WithFailSafe`, `WithFailSafeTimeout` and
`WithFailSafeRetryAfter`. `CacheWhen<T>` is configured in code for one method; a `CacheWhen<T>` for a type the method
can't return, such as `CacheWhen<string>` on a method that returns `int`, throws an `InvalidOperationException` at
startup (an `ArgumentException` from a runtime override) instead of silently caching nothing. Cache callbacks and
context predicates are not supported.

`[Cache]` takes named settings only. `Enabled` and `Distributed` inherit the configured policy when you leave them out,
and an explicit `false` wins over the lower layers. `FailSafeRetryAfter` sets how long a served fail-safe value is
reused before the method is tried again (30 seconds by default). `[assembly: CacheInterface(typeof(...), nameof(...))]`
takes the same named settings.

Overloaded generic methods have the number of type parameters in their method id: `Get(int)`, `Get``1(int)` and
`Get``2(int)` are three methods, in `appsettings.json` as well. Options and tags you pass in code are copied, so
changing the collection afterwards changes nothing.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/manual-caching.md -->

# Manual caching

When an attribute doesn't fit, such as a call in the middle of a method or a client without an interface, use the same
cache through `ICacheManager` with a key you choose:

```cs
public sealed class OrderReader(ICacheManager cache, IOrderRepository orders)
{
    public ValueTask<Order> GetAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct = default) =>
        cache.GetOrCreateAsync(
            $"order:{id}",
            async token => await orders.GetAsync(id, token),
            o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30)).AddTags("orders", $"order:{id}"),
            cancellationToken: ct);
}
```

It shares the in-memory cache, the distributed cache, stampede protection and invalidation with `[Cache]` methods.

## Keys

You always pass the key yourself. MethodCache doesn't derive keys from the lambda, so a captured variable never ends
up in a key by accident, and two calls share an entry only when their keys are equal. Use a prefix per kind of data,
such as `order:42`, so keys from different places can't collide. An empty or whitespace key throws
`ArgumentException`.

## Options

`GetOrCreateAsync` takes every option, including a predicate that only makes sense per call:

```cs
var list = await cache.GetOrCreateAsync(
    $"orders:{customerId}:{status}",
    async ct => await orders.ListAsync(customerId, status, ct),
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30))
          .WithSlidingExpiration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10))
          .WithRefreshAhead(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5))
          .AddTags("orders", $"customer:{customerId}")
          .WithVersion(2)
          .WithEnabled(customerId > 0));   // skip the cache when false
```

- Duration, sliding expiration, refresh-ahead, tags and version work as described in [Expiration](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/expiration.md) and
  [Invalidation](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/invalidation.md).
- `WithEnabled(false)` runs the factory on every call, and neither reads nor stores the entry.
- `WithDistributed(false)` uses memory only. `CacheWhen<T>` checks the result before it is stored, and a value read
  from the distributed cache.
- On a hot path, build the options once and reuse them: `static readonly CacheEntryOptions Options = new CacheEntryOptions.Builder().WithDuration(...).Build();`
  and pass `Options` instead of a builder action, so a call doesn't build options again.
- To avoid a closure, `ICacheManager.GetOrCreateAsync(key, state, (state, ct) => ..., options)` passes your state to a
  static factory.
- Configuration files and runtime overrides apply to declared cached methods. Explicit-key calls use their own options.
- `Build()` copies the tags, so changing the builder afterwards changes nothing.

`ICacheManager` has four operations: `GetOrCreateAsync`, `TryGetAsync`, `InvalidateKeysAsync` and
`InvalidateTagsAsync`. The interface takes every argument; extension methods give the short forms, such as
`TryGetAsync<T>(key, cancellationToken)`, `InvalidateKeyAsync(key)` and `InvalidateKeyAsync(key, version)`, and take a
builder action instead of built options. To write your own manager, see
[Registration](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/reference/registration.md#your-own-cache-manager).

## Reading without loading

```cs
var lookup = await cache.TryGetAsync<Order>("order:42");
if (lookup.Found)
{
    Console.WriteLine(lookup.Value);
}
```

`TryGetAsync` takes the `version` an entry was stored with: `TryGetAsync<Order>("order:42", 2)`.

## Versions and the stored key

An entry stored with `WithVersion` lives under a different key than the unversioned one: `entry` at version 1 never
shares a value with the key `entry::v1`. `TryGetAsync` and `InvalidateKeyAsync` take the same key and version you
cached with: `TryGetAsync<Order>("order:42", 2)`, `InvalidateKeyAsync("order:42", 2)`.
`ICacheAdministrator` takes the stored key, `MethodCacheKeys.StoredKey(key, version)`, which is what
`CacheEntryInfo.StoredKey` shows; treat its format as opaque. To invalidate a versioned entry through `ICacheManager`,
pass the key and its version, `InvalidateKeyAsync(key, 2)`, not the stored key.

## Many keys at once

`GetOrCreateManyAsync` checks the local cache for every key, looks up the local misses in the distributed cache,
and calls the factory once with the keys neither holds. Each key gets the value the cache selects: memory first, then
the distributed cache, then the factory. A bulk read therefore agrees with individual reads of the same keys, even
across nodes: a value another node stored in the distributed cache is returned as is, and its key is not passed to
the factory. A concurrent writer may still win over a value the factory produced; the returned dictionary then holds
the writer's value, as an individual read would:

```cs
var users = await cache.GetOrCreateManyAsync<User>(
    userIds.Select(id => $"user:{id}"),
    async (missingKeys, ct) =>
    {
        var ids = missingKeys.Select(k => int.Parse(k["user:".Length..])).ToList();
        var loaded = await repository.GetUsersAsync(ids, ct);   // one query for all misses
        return loaded.ToDictionary(u => $"user:{u.Id}", u => u);
    },
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromHours(1)));
```

- The factory returns an `IReadOnlyDictionary` with a value for each key it gets, and the call returns one for every
  key. An answer that leaves out a key, or is `null`, fails like a factory that throws, and none of its values is
  cached.
- On a hot path, build the options once and pass the `CacheEntryOptions` instead of a builder action.
- Each key behaves as `GetOrCreateAsync` would for it. When the factory throws, each key it was asked for gets its
  fail-safe value; when a key has none, the factory's exception is thrown.
- `cancellationToken` stops this caller's wait. A factory that ignores it finishes in the background, and its values
  are cached unless they were invalidated while it ran.

## Things to know

- Concurrent calls for the same key share one factory run. A caller's `cancellationToken` stops its own wait; if it
  cancels a run others joined, they run the factory again rather than fail.
- A factory that asks for the key it is loading (itself, or through the cached service it belongs to) would wait for
  itself, so that call throws an `InvalidOperationException` instead, and the key is free for the next caller.
- To cache a sequence, materialize it in the factory (`await query.ToListAsync(ct)`) and cache the list.
- The four operations on `ICacheManager` can be mocked directly. The options-builder convenience overload
  delegates to that interface. You can also pass a `NoOpCacheManager` ([Testing](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/testing.md)).

- `TryGetAsync` returns a fresh entry, a cached `null` included, also when refresh-ahead is due; it never runs a
  factory or starts a refresh.
- An entry invalidated while `GetOrCreateManyAsync`'s factory runs is returned to that caller but not stored.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/third-party.md -->

# Caching third-party code

MethodCache can cache calls to code you don't own, such as API clients, cloud SDKs or payment gateways, to cut API
costs and latency. Pick one of three approaches:

| Approach | Best for |
|----------|----------|
| `[assembly: CacheInterface]` | A client that ships an interface: cache chosen methods with one line, no wrapper |
| A wrapper interface with `[Cache]` | A client without an interface (a sealed class or static methods) |
| `ICacheManager.GetOrCreateAsync` | One or two calls, or keys you want to build yourself |

## The client's own interface

Name the interface and the methods to cache in an assembly attribute, anywhere in your project:

```cs
[assembly: CacheInterface(typeof(IFxRatesClient), nameof(IFxRatesClient.GetRateAsync),
    Duration = "00:01:00", Tags = ["fx", "fx:{from}"])]
```

```cs
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IFxRatesClient, FxRatesClient>();   // the vendor's client, registered as usual
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
```

- The listed methods behave like methods with `[Cache]`: keys from the arguments, tag templates with the method's
  parameter names, zero-allocation hits on .NET 10. Methods you don't list always reach the client, so writes
  are never cached by accident.
- The attribute's settings (`Duration`, `Tags`, `Group`, `SlidingExpiration`, `RefreshAhead`, `Version`, `FailSafe`,
  `FailSafeTimeout`, `FailSafeRetryAfter`, `Enabled`, `Distributed`) apply to every listed method. Give one method its
  own settings like any cached method:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(config => config.Method((IFxRatesClient c) => c.GetRateAsync(Any<string>.Value, Any<string>.Value))
    .Configure(o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))));
```

- The method id in `appsettings.json` and the admin endpoints is the name of the assembly that declares the interface
  (the vendor's, not yours) in brackets, the interface's full name, a dot and the method name, for example
  `[FxVendor]FxVendor.IFxRatesClient.GetRateAsync`. `IMethodCacheKeys.MethodId` returns it for you.
- List each interface once. It must be non-generic and come from another assembly; for your own interfaces, put
  `[Cache]` on the methods. A method with overloads can't be listed yet.
- The attribute can live in a class library, such as your infrastructure project. Select its generated module
  explicitly with `MethodCacheBuilder.FromAssemblyOf<T>()`, using a type declared in that assembly. This bootstraps
  the module under Native AOT without relying on discovery of loaded assemblies; your own `[Cache]` interfaces in
  other assemblies stay cached.
- When multiple assemblies generate the same interface, the module you select wins. Calling and entry assemblies
  have no special precedence. An ambiguous registration throws `InvalidOperationException` naming the candidates.

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(cache => cache.FromAssemblyOf<Rates>());
```

- Mistakes are build errors: [MC0011](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0011) (a type it can't cache, such as one with
  static abstract or non-public abstract members), [MC0012](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0012) (a method that is
  missing, overloaded, static, or one `[Cache]` would reject) and [MC0013](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0013) (an
  interface listed twice).

## A wrapper interface

Define an interface in your project with the calls you need, and put the settings on it:

```cs
public interface IRates
{
    [Cache(Duration = "00:01:00", Tags = ["fx", "fx:{from}"])]
    Task<decimal> GetAsync(string from, string to);
}

public sealed class Rates(FxRatesClient client) : IRates   // calls the vendor's concrete class
{
    public Task<decimal> GetAsync(string from, string to) => client.GetRateAsync(from, to);
}
```

```cs
builder.Services.AddSingleton<FxRatesClient>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IRates, Rates>();
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
```

Static methods and sealed classes work the same way: the wrapper calls them, and the interface carries the attributes.

## An explicit key

```cs
var rate = await cache.GetOrCreateAsync(
    $"fx:{from}:{to}",
    async ct => await client.GetRateAsync(from, to),
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1)).AddTags("fx"));
```

See [Manual caching](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/manual-caching.md).

## Things to know

- **Leave writes uncached.** Payments, uploads and deletes must not be cached; mark wrapper methods that change data
  with `[CacheInvalidate(Tags = ...)]`.
- **Exceptions are not cached.** With [fail-safe](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/fail-safe.md) on, the previous value is served while the client
  fails.
- **Invalidate from a webhook** with `cache.InvalidateTagAsync("fx:EUR")` when the vendor tells you data changed.
- **Share results between instances** with a [distributed cache](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/distributed-cache.md) when every instance calls the
  same paid API.
- **Start with short durations** and lengthen them once you know how fresh the data must be.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/http-caching.md -->

# HTTP response caching

Add `AddHttpCaching()` to an `HttpClient` registration to cache HTTP responses according to their response headers,
as RFC 9111 describes. Freshness comes from `Cache-Control` and expiry headers; `ETag` and `Last-Modified` enable
conditional validation, and a successful 304 is returned to the caller as the full response.

Chapter 11 of the [console tour](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/samples/MethodCache.Demo#httpclient-caching) starts a local HTTP server and checks cache hits, ETag/304 validation, `no-store` and invalidation after PUT. It needs no external API or Docker.

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<IGitHubClient, GitHubClient>()
    .AddHttpCaching();
```

The [package guide](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.HttpCaching/README.md) covers settings, private and shared caches, limits
and metrics. This page covers the rules the cache follows. [Security](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/security.md#methodcachehttpcaching) has the
threat model, and the [HTTP caching reference](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/reference/http-caching.md) the exact behavior.

## Freshness and validation

- Stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error are optional. Response `no-cache` requires successful validation before
  the response is reused, even when either option is on. Request `no-cache` has the same requirement: a 5xx response
  or network error reaches the caller rather than falling back to cached content.
- `must-revalidate` forbids serving a stale response, as do `proxy-revalidate` and `s-maxage` in a shared cache.
- An `Expires` at or before the response `Date`, or one that doesn't parse (such as `Expires: 0`), makes the response
  stale at once. Heuristic freshness and `DefaultMaxAge` don't extend it. An explicit `max-age` (or `s-maxage` in a
  shared cache) wins over `Expires`.
- A 304 updates the stored response's headers and whether it may be stored. If it changes to `no-store`, `Vary: *`, or
  `private` in a shared cache, the stored response is removed. This applies to background revalidation too. A 304
  without `Vary` keeps the original variant selection. If the updated response can't be stored, the old one is
  removed so its old rules are never used again; the caller still gets the response. If removing it fails too, the
  error reaches the caller.
- A `Cache-Control` or `Vary` field that doesn't parse (such as `private; max-age=600` or `max-age=-1`), also next to a valid one, is not
  read as absent: the response is not stored, because the header may have said `private` or `no-store`.
- An entry is kept at most a year, even when `Expires` is far in the future (`31 Dec 9999`).
- Weak ETags (`W/"abc"`) are sent back as weak validators.
- `only-if-cached` never contacts the origin, including for range requests, requests with their own validators,
  `no-store`, methods that aren't cached and background revalidation. When no stored response can be used, the
  answer is 504.

## Redirects, retries and request bodies

- A redirect the transport follows (`AllowAutoRedirect`, the default) answers a different URL, so it is not stored
  under the URL you requested. The transport also drops `Authorization` on a redirect, so storing it could hand one
  caller's response to another. Requests that end at the redirect target are cached under that URL as usual. If the
  target answers the cache's own validators with 304, the request is sent again without them, so you get the full response.
  A URL that was cached and now redirects has its stored response removed, also when background revalidation finds out.
- The cache stores responses for the request as you sent it, before the transport adds headers such as
  `Accept-Encoding` for automatic decompression. `Vary: Accept-Encoding` therefore works with `AutomaticDecompression`.
- The `If-None-Match` / `If-Modified-Since` headers the cache adds are removed again before the response is
  returned, so a retry handler (Polly, standard resilience) that sends the same message again gets a full response.
- A `GET` or `HEAD` with a body (search APIs such as Elasticsearch) goes to the origin: its URL doesn't identify it.
- The URL fragment (`#top`) is not part of the key; it never reaches the origin.

## Writes and invalidation

- A successful `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` invalidates the cached responses for its URL before it returns: the
  URL you sent it to, also when the response redirects (`303 See Other`) elsewhere. A `GET` already in flight can't
  store its older response over it.
- With Redis, SQL Server or PostgreSQL configured, every instance sees the invalidation at once, even when backplane
  messages are lost.
- If the invalidation can't be confirmed, the call throws `HttpCacheInvalidationException`. The write may have
  succeeded at the origin, so don't retry it automatically. A `GET` that throws it is safe to retry.
- To invalidate from code, use `ICacheAdministrator`: one response by the id `ListEntries` gives, a client's
  responses by its tag (`http:` followed by `MethodCacheKeys.Part(clientName)`) or the tags in `HttpCacheOptions.Tags`,
  or everything with `ClearAsync`.

## Storage

Responses are stored in MethodCache's memory cache, in a budget of their own (`MaxHttpBytes`, 100 MiB by default,
headers included) next to method results. With Redis, SQL Server or PostgreSQL configured, they are stored there
instead, so every instance shares them. A response larger than the budget is streamed to the caller and not stored.
`AddHttpCaching` needs `AddMethodCache` in the same container, in either order. The admin endpoints and
`ICacheAdministrator` list and remove cached responses; they never show bodies, credentials, cookies or query strings.

## Transport and cookies

`AddHttpCaching()` turns off automatic cookies on the client's `SocketsHttpHandler` or `HttpClientHandler`, after all
other configuration of that handler, so the default registration caches at once. Other named clients are unaffected.
A handler that already has cookies off is left alone, so a cookie-free handler shared between clients keeps working.
`ConfigureHttpClientDefaults(b => b.AddHttpCaching())` caches every client, each under its own name: two clients
never share entries, and they all use the settings given there. A client has at most one cache: calling
`AddHttpCaching` again for one client, or twice, adds no second cache and applies every settings delegate. To give
one client other settings, use `services.Configure<HttpCacheOptions>("name", o => ...)`.
`KeepCookies=true` leaves the transport's cookies on and turns response caching, validation and stale fallback off for
that client. `only-if-cached` then returns 504, and a successful write still invalidates its URL.
Send caller cookies as request headers; a handler that keeps a hidden cookie jar belongs on a client without HTTP
caching.

The cache runs after every other handler you add, so caller identity and rewritten requests are visible before
lookup.

Other transports (wrappers the cache can't see into, native platform handlers), and handlers inside the primary
transport or below a cache handler you construct yourself, can't be checked. They bypass caching and log one warning
per named client, unless you set `AllowUnverifiedTransport`. Set it only when you have checked that the whole
transport sends no automatic cookies or hidden caller identity. A known transport with automatic cookies turned on
always bypasses.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/distributed-cache.md -->

# Distributed cache

By default each application instance has its own in-memory cache. Add a distributed cache to share results between
instances and keep them across restarts:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc.UseRedis("localhost:6379"));   // MethodCache.Redis
```

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc.UseSqlServer(connectionString));   // MethodCache.SqlServer
```

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc.UsePostgreSql(connectionString));   // MethodCache.PostgreSql
```

The [web demo](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/samples/MethodCache.WebDemo) runs two instances that share Redis, including what happens when
Redis goes down.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A([Call a cached method]):::dark --> B{In memory?}
    B -- yes --> R([Return the value]):::amber
    B -- no --> C{In Redis, SQL Server<br/>or PostgreSQL?}
    C -- yes --> D[Keep it in memory]:::light --> R
    C -- no --> E[Run your method]:::dark --> F[Write it to memory<br/>and the distributed cache]:::light --> R
    classDef dark fill:#1E1B3A,stroke:#1E1B3A,color:#F5F3FF
    classDef amber fill:#FFB020,stroke:#FFB020,color:#1E1B3A
    classDef light fill:#F5F3FF,stroke:#1E1B3A,color:#1E1B3A
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Instance A
    participant D as Redis / SQL Server / PostgreSQL
    participant B as Instance B
    A->>A: [CacheInvalidate] or InvalidateTagsAsync
    A->>D: Remove the key, or stamp the tag
    A-->>B: Backplane message (pub/sub, NOTIFY, or the next poll)
    B->>B: Drop the in-memory copy
    Note over B: The next call reads the distributed cache or runs the method
```

- Results live in memory and in the distributed cache. An in-memory miss reads the distributed cache before
  running your method, and a new result is written to both.
- Invalidating a key removes it from the distributed cache. Invalidating a tag records when it happened, so older
  entries with that tag read as misses. A backplane tells every other instance to drop its in-memory copy: at once
  with Redis pub/sub and PostgreSQL `NOTIFY`, or on their next poll (every second by default) with SQL Server.
- Redis, Microsoft SQL Server and PostgreSQL are supported. Other stores are not; the storage interfaces are
  internal. Use one of them: calling more than one of `UseRedis`, `UseSqlServer` and `UsePostgreSql` throws.
  `Distributed(...)` and `UseMessagePack()` without one log a warning at startup, since they have nothing to apply to.
- `[Cache]` methods and `GetOrCreateAsync` need no changes. Synchronous `[Cache]` methods use only the memory cache,
  so they never wait on the network; a synchronous `[CacheInvalidate]` reaches the other instances in the background.
- MethodCache keeps its own distributed cache and connection, so your application's `IDistributedCache` is left alone
  and is never used as a fallback.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Run the same MethodCache version on every instance that shares a cache and backplane; messages from another version
> are ignored with one warning.

## When the distributed cache is down

Calls keep working from memory and your methods; the distributed cache never fails or stalls a call. Each call to it
is capped at `OperationTimeout` (one second), a circuit breaker skips it until it is back, and invalidations are queued and retried
instead of throwing. Until they are stored, the instance doesn't read entries from it, so an invalidated value can't
come back. The [health check](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/monitoring.md#health-check) reports Degraded while this lasts.

Queued invalidations are stored a batch at a time once the cache answers, so a long outage's backlog drains at the
pace the cache can take. More than 10,000 are replaced by one clear of the distributed cache (logged as a warning),
and so is an invalidation the cache keeps refusing while it answers everything else, so neither holds up the rest.
The queue lives in memory: when the instance shuts down, it waits for writes still running, then tries once more to store
what is queued, each step (stamp, removal, publish) capped by `OperationTimeout`, and logs a warning with the number it had to drop. Other instances can read those invalidated
values from the distributed cache until they expire.

A value set directly while the distributed cache is down stays in that instance's memory, and the value it replaced is
removed from the distributed cache and the other instances once it is back. An entry that comes back damaged (cut
short, or unreadable by the serializer) is a miss: your method runs and its result replaces the entry.

The timeout caps each call to the distributed cache, not a whole cache miss. A cache that stops answering costs a miss
one timeout, after which the circuit breaker skips it. One that answers just within the timeout costs a miss up to
three: reading the entry, writing your method's result and checking that no removal raced the write (and a fourth for
the backplane message).

## Options

`DistributedCacheOptions` apply to Redis, SQL Server and PostgreSQL alike:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc.Distributed(options =>
{
    options.OperationTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500);
    options.CircuitBreakerDuration = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
}));
```

| Option | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `OperationTimeout` | 1 second | The longest one call to the distributed cache may take. A slower call is abandoned and counts as a failure, except a write (see [What other instances see](#what-other-instances-see)) |
| `CircuitBreakerDuration` | 10 seconds | How long the distributed cache is skipped after a failure or timeout. Invalidations it didn't accept are retried at this interval |
| `ClockSkewTolerance` | 2 seconds | How far apart your servers' clocks may be. A tag invalidation also applies to entries created up to this long after it. One stamped further ahead of an instance's clock (by a server whose clock runs fast) counts from when that instance first read it, until its clock reaches the stamp |
| `TagCheckInterval` | 1 second | How long an instance trusts the invalidation time it last read for a tag. Without a backplane, an entry read from the distributed cache can outlive a tag invalidation made on another instance by up to this long |
| `TagRetention` | 1 day | How long tag invalidations are kept. An entry stays in the distributed cache at most `TagRetention - ClockSkewTolerance` from when your method started loading it (less if its own duration is shorter); a load that takes longer is kept only in that instance's memory. Both values are truncated to whole milliseconds, and `TagRetention` must exceed `ClockSkewTolerance` by at least one millisecond, or startup fails; with SQL Server it must also end before 9999-12-31 |
| `KeyPrefix` | `methodcache:` | The prefix of everything MethodCache stores and of its backplane messages. Give each application that shares a store its own. It can't change while the app runs |
| `VerifyRoundTrip` | `true` | Read each value back before sharing it, and keep values that don't come back the same in memory only ([Serialization](#serialization)) |
| `SerializerVersion` | `1` | Raise it when you change serializer settings, so values written with the old settings are not read |

## Invalidations only

When each process should keep its own values, and only needs to hear about invalidations (a worker that changes data
an API caches, say), turn off the distributed cache for every method. Values stay in each process's memory, and every
invalidation still reaches the other processes:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc
    .UsePostgreSql(connectionString)
    .Defaults(o => o.WithDistributed(false)));   // values stay in memory; invalidations reach every process
```

Invalidations are still stored in the database, so it needs the same tables as a full distributed cache, but no
values are written there.

## What other instances see

- An invalidation reaches another instance when the backplane delivers it, usually within milliseconds; until then
  that instance serves its in-memory copy. Instances without a copy read the distributed cache, which is already
  right. When an instance loses its backplane connection:
  - With SQL Server and PostgreSQL, invalidations are rows in a table, so the instance reads the ones it missed when
    it reconnects. An instance that couldn't read the table for half of `BackplaneRetention` may have missed some, so
    it clears its whole in-memory cache.
  - With Redis, a message reaches only the instances connected when it is sent, so the instance clears its whole
    in-memory cache when its connection comes back.
  - With `EnableBackplane = false`, no instance hears of another's invalidations: each serves its in-memory copy until
    it expires.
- Messages carry no values, so a late, repeated or reordered message only makes an instance read the distributed cache
  again.
- An invalidation the distributed cache didn't accept is retried every `CircuitBreakerDuration`. Until the retry
  succeeds, other instances can serve the old value; the instance that invalidated never does.
- A write that timed out (a large value, say) doesn't open the circuit breaker, since the cache may answer everything
  else: the instance logs a warning and keeps using it. Such a write may still land later, because a distributed cache
  has no compare-and-set, so its key is removed again after `CircuitBreakerDuration` (as after a write that failed,
  once the cache answers). Further timed-out writes of the key push that one removal back, and an instance that shuts
  down first removes the key while it shuts down. Until then the late value can replace a newer one, and a write that
  lands after that removal stays until it expires.
- Entries carry no checksum: damage that still reads as a valid value is served.

## Serialization

Values are written as JSON with System.Text.Json, public fields included, so records, value tuples and structs are
shared as they are. Each value is read back once before it is shared. A value that doesn't come back the same, such as
a class with private setters, a `Dog` returned from a method declared to return `Animal`, or `object`, stays in that
instance's memory only, with one warning that names the method and the type. Register your own
`JsonSerializerOptions` or `JsonSerializerContext` with `UseJson` to share such values (`[JsonInclude]`,
`[JsonDerivedType]`). [Distributed cache reference](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/reference/distributed.md#serialization) has the exact rules.

The `MethodCache.Serialization.MessagePack` package makes values smaller and faster to read:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc
    .UseRedis("localhost:6379")
    .UseMessagePack());   // MethodCache.Serialization.MessagePack
```

Entries written in the other format read as misses and are replaced, so switching needs no flush. See the
[MessagePack package guide](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.Serialization.MessagePack/README.md). Under Native AOT, register your
`JsonSerializerContext` ([Native AOT](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/native-aot.md)).

## Keep invalidations from being evicted

> [!WARNING]
> Tag, clear and key-removal stamps are ordinary expiring keys next to the entries they invalidate. A store that evicts a
> stamp under memory pressure while an entry it invalidated stays makes that entry valid again, on every instance, until
> it expires. Give the store room, and don't let it evict MethodCache's keys: for Redis, use `maxmemory-policy
> noeviction` (or a Redis of its own). Every MethodCache key has a time to live, so the `volatile-*` policies can evict
> them as well as the `allkeys-*` ones. With `noeviction`, a full Redis refuses writes instead: MethodCache then treats it
> as down and answers from memory. SQL Server and PostgreSQL remove rows only once they expired.

## Changing result types and upgrading

- Raise the method's `Version` (or `SerializerVersion` for serializer settings) when a cached result's shape changes,
  so values the previous version wrote are not read.
- Run the same MethodCache version on every instance that shares a store.
- SQL Server and PostgreSQL create their tables on first use. With an existing SQL Server invalidations table from
  before 1.0, or a login that may not create tables, see the
  [SQL Server](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.SqlServer/README.md) and [PostgreSQL](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.PostgreSql/README.md) guides.

## Limits

- Invalidation matches exact keys and tags; common tags provide group invalidation.
- [Fail-safe](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/fail-safe.md) values and [runtime overrides](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md#runtime-overrides) live in each instance's
  memory.

## Package guides

The [Redis](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.Redis/README.md), [SQL Server](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.SqlServer/README.md) and
[PostgreSQL](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.PostgreSql/README.md) READMEs cover their options, shared connections, table creation,
outage settings and how each stores keys and invalidations. The PostgreSQL guide compares all three; the SQL Server
guide has the schema migration for an existing invalidations table. [Benchmarks](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/benchmarks.md#distributed-cache-providers)
measures them side by side. The exact guarantees, such as what a cancelled call leaves behind and how each
backplane recovers, are in the [distributed cache reference](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/reference/distributed.md).


---

<!-- source: docs/features/monitoring.md -->

# Monitoring

Core emits standard .NET metrics and activities. `AddMethodCache()` uses the container's `IMeterFactory`, registering
one when needed, and owns an `ActivitySource` with the same `MethodCacheTelemetry.Name` (`MethodCache`). Both use the
assembly version. Separate containers keep their observation callbacks separate.

## Administration and statistics

`ICacheAdministrator`, registered for the built-in manager, exposes local statistics, methods and entries:

```cs
var stats = await admin.GetStatsAsync();
var ratio = stats.Hits + stats.Misses == 0 ? 0 : (double)stats.Hits / (stats.Hits + stats.Misses);
Console.WriteLine($"Hit ratio {ratio:P0}, {stats.LocalMethodEntries} local method entries");
Console.WriteLine($"HTTP: {stats.LocalHttpEntries} local responses, {stats.LocalHttpBytes} stored bytes");
Console.WriteLine($"Method weight: {stats.TotalWeight} (configured weight units)");

foreach (var method in admin.GetMethods())
    Console.WriteLine($"{method.MethodId}: {method.Options.Duration}");

var entries = admin.ListEntries(tag: "user:42");
await admin.InvalidateTagsAsync(["user:42"]);
```

`Hits`, `Misses` and `Evictions` are local counters. Compute a hit ratio in the app or dashboard. Storage fields have
explicit scopes:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `LocalMethodEntries` | Method results resident in this instance |
| `LocalHttpEntries` | HTTP representations resident in this instance |
| `LocalHttpBytes` | HTTP storage cost in bytes; separate from method weight |
| `ObservedDistributedEntries` | HTTP responses this instance recently saw in the distributed cache (at most 1024); not a count of what is stored there |
| `TotalWeight` | Resident method weight in the configured weigher's units; one per entry without a weigher |

Statistics never serialize results or inspect their properties to estimate bytes. HTTP storage/observation fields
remain zero until the separate HTTP store is registered.

`GetMethods()` returns each method's `MethodId`, its effective `Options`, the `SettingSources` each setting comes from
and `IsDistributedNamespaceShared`. `ListEntries(storedKeyPrefix, tag, limit, methodId)` and `GetEntry(storedKey)`
inspect live local entries without values; listing is a diagnostic scan, not a transaction. `CacheEntryInfo.MethodId`
names the method an entry belongs to (`null` for manual entries and HTTP responses), and `ListEntries(methodId: ...)`
lists exactly that method's entries. `IMethodCacheKeys.MethodId` returns the id of a call ([Cache keys](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/keys.md)).
`CacheEntryInfo.StoredKey` is the key as stored, which `GetEntry` and `RemoveEntryAsync` take. For a manual entry with a
`Version` it includes the version, so it is not the key you pass to `ICacheManager`; there, use the key and version you
cached it with. `InvalidateMethodAsync(methodId)` removes every entry of one method, on every instance; an id no
cached method has throws an `ArgumentException`. `RemoveEntryAsync`, `InvalidateTagsAsync`, `InvalidateMethodAsync`
and `ClearAsync` complete once a configured distributed cache has confirmed the change, and throw
`CacheInvalidationQueuedException` when it is applied in memory but still queued for the distributed cache. Its
`Result` holds the counts of the invalidation (`null` for `ClearAsync`). The cache retries on its own; don't repeat
the call. `GetInvalidationQueues()` reports `Queued` (waiting for the distributed cache) and `PublicationQueued`
(waiting for the backplane). A custom or NoOp manager has no built-in method administrator or fabricated storage
statistics; with `AddHttpCaching` there is one for HTTP responses only.

## Admin endpoints

The `MethodCache.AspNetCore` package exposes administration behind an explicit authorization policy:

```cs
builder.Services.AddScoped<IUserService, UserService>();
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks().AddMethodCache();
builder.Services.AddAuthorization(o => o.AddPolicy("CacheAdmins", p => p.RequireRole("Admin")));

var app = builder.Build();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapMethodCacheAdmin("CacheAdmins");
app.MapHealthChecks("/health");
```

The [package README](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.AspNetCore/README.md#endpoints) lists the endpoints. Policies are read-only;
use [runtime overrides](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md#runtime-overrides) to change them.

Configure your application's authentication scheme as well as the authorization policy. The
[web demo](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/samples/MethodCache.WebDemo) uses cookies and returns 401 for anonymous admin requests and
403 for signed-in callers without the `Admin` role outside Development. It has no sign-in page; its
Development environment allows anonymous admin requests so you can try the endpoints locally.
It also exposes Development-only `/demo/queries` and `/demo/reset` routes to count source reads and restore
the demonstration data; those routes are not part of the MethodCache admin package.
## Health check

`AddHealthChecks().AddMethodCache()` reports the selected `failureStatus` (default `Degraded`) when the distributed cache doesn't answer,
invalidations are waiting to be retried, or the backplane is connecting or disconnected. The distributed cache and the
backplane are reported separately. Reports include `managerCapability`,
`statisticsAvailable`, `distributedCacheAvailable` when applicable, `backplaneStatus`, `queued` and
`publicationQueued`, plus local storage statistics; the
[package README](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.AspNetCore/README.md#health-check) lists every key. Backend exception text is
omitted.

An incompatible distributed schema or retention contract reports `Unhealthy` with an actionable safe reason,
uses local memory only, and retains invalidations. A safe established retention differing from the configured
value reports `Degraded`. Admin mutations return 503 when distributed storage has not confirmed invalidation;
the cache continues owning retries.

An empty queue and a connected subscription do not acknowledge delivery to every node; backplane delivery remains
best effort.

## OpenTelemetry

The optional `MethodCache.OpenTelemetry` package provides `AddMethodCacheInstrumentation()` on meter and tracer
builders. These extensions only subscribe to Core's instruments; they do not wrap, replace or take ownership of your
manager. SDK setup may precede or follow `AddMethodCache()`, and repeated subscriptions do not multiply events.

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();

builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry()
    .WithTracing(tracing => tracing
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddMethodCacheInstrumentation()
        .AddOtlpExporter())
    .WithMetrics(metrics => metrics
        .AddMethodCacheInstrumentation()
        .AddOtlpExporter());
```

Each completed cache call has one `methodcache.requests` outcome, `methodcache.result`: `hit`, `miss`, `stale`,
`revalidated`, `bypass` or `error`. `methodcache.kind` is `method`, `manual` or `http`, and `methodcache.method` (a
method id) or `methodcache.http.client` (a client name) says which; manual calls by key carry neither. Every attribute
is in the `methodcache.` namespace, apart from `error.type`. `methodcache.load.duration` measures your method when it
actually runs, background refreshes included; callers that join a running load and values read from the distributed
cache record none. A bulk call has one outcome and measures its one batch factory call.

Histograms use seconds, with bucket boundaries from 5 ms to 10 s. Local entry/HTTP byte instruments are observable
up-down counters. Invalidation counters count
distinct targets at each stage, not operation totals; do not add stages together. See the
[full instrument table](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.OpenTelemetry/README.md#metrics).

Spans cover runs of your method, individual distributed operations and invalidation. Pure hits have no spans. Keys
and tags require explicit Core options; keys are hashed by default when enabled. Metrics never include keys, tags,
URLs, user ids or tenant ids. MethodCache adds no baggage and copies no HTTP or URL attributes; your application's
own activity context and baggage flow as usual.

## Standard .NET listeners

OpenTelemetry is optional. The meter and activity source are named `MethodCache` (`MethodCacheTelemetry.Name`), so
`dotnet-counters monitor --counters MethodCache` and any `MeterListener` see them. For Prometheus, use OpenTelemetry's
Prometheus exporter with `AddMethodCacheInstrumentation()`. A `MeterListener` subscribes like this; keep it alive for
as long as you want measurements:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
using var listener = new MeterListener();
listener.InstrumentPublished = (instrument, active) =>
{
    if (instrument.Meter.Name == MethodCacheTelemetry.Name)
        active.EnableMeasurementEvents(instrument);
};
listener.SetMeasurementEventCallback<long>((instrument, value, _, _) =>
    Console.WriteLine($"{instrument.Name}: {value}"));
listener.Start(); // keep the listener alive for as long as measurements are needed
```

The privacy options are set in `AddMethodCache` and apply whatever listens:

```cs
// Core emits standard Meter and ActivitySource instruments
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc.Telemetry(options =>
{
    options.RecordCacheKeys = false;
    options.RecordCacheTags = false;
}));
```

With your own `ICacheManager`, MethodCache still measures whether a cached method's factory ran; anything else your
manager does is its own to instrument.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/memory-cache.md -->

# Memory cache

The in-memory cache uses W-TinyLFU eviction: when it is full, it keeps the entries that are read often and
evicts the rest, so a burst of one-off reads doesn't push out your hot data. Configure it with
`mc.Memory(o => ...)`, which sets `MethodCacheMemoryOptions`:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(cache => cache
    .Defaults(o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10)))
    .Memory(o =>
    {
        o.MaxItems = 50_000;                              // default 10,000
        o.JitterMaxDuration = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);   // spread out entries created together
        o.CacheNullValues = false;                        // a null result means "try again next time"
    }));
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| `MaxItems` | 10,000 | The most entries kept, also when a `Weigher` is set |
| `WeightLimit` | 1000 MB | The most total weight kept; needs a `Weigher` |
| `Weigher` | none | Returns an entry's cost, for example its size in bytes |
| `MaxExpiration` | 7 days | No entry lives longer: a longer `Duration` fails where it is set. At most 365 days |
| `JitterMaxDuration` | zero | Adds a random extra lifetime up to this value, so entries created together don't expire together |
| `CacheNullValues` | `true` | Caches `null` results like any other value |
| `MaxHttpBytes` | 100 MiB | The most bytes the HTTP response cache keeps in memory, bodies and headers included. Shared by all HTTP clients and separate from `MaxItems` and `WeightLimit` |

Method defaults are set with `Defaults.WithDuration`; unset defaults use five minutes. Cleanup, statistics and
the generated fast path are always enabled.

## How a call is answered

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A([Call a cached method]):::dark --> B{In memory?}
    B -- yes --> R([Return the same instance]):::amber
    B -- no --> C[Concurrent callers with the<br/>same key share one call]:::light
    C --> E[Run your method]:::dark
    E -- returns --> F[Store it, unless CacheWhen<br/>or CacheNullValues rejects it]:::light --> R
    E -- throws --> X(["Nothing is stored: the caller gets<br/>the exception or a fail-safe value"]):::dark
    classDef dark fill:#1E1B3A,stroke:#1E1B3A,color:#F5F3FF
    classDef amber fill:#FFB020,stroke:#FFB020,color:#1E1B3A
    classDef light fill:#F5F3FF,stroke:#1E1B3A,color:#1E1B3A
```

## Bounding by size

Object sizes can't be measured reliably at runtime, so to bound the cache by memory you say what an entry costs:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(cache => cache.Memory(o =>
{
    o.WeightLimit = 256 * 1024 * 1024;   // bound the cache by total size as well as by count
    o.Weigher = (key, value) => value is string s ? s.Length * 2 : 64;
}));
```

The weigher must be fast, thread-safe and return a non-negative value. Both limits apply: an entry is evicted as soon
as either `MaxItems` or `WeightLimit` is reached, so raise `MaxItems` too when many small entries should fit. Setting
`WeightLimit` without a `Weigher` fails at startup, since there is nothing to weigh entries with.

## Memory statistics

`GetStatsAsync().TotalWeight` reports the resident method weight in the configured weigher's units. Without a
weigher, every method entry weighs one; a large returned object does not turn this field into bytes.
`LocalMethodEntries` reports the actual local entry count. Statistics never serialize results or inspect user
properties, and there are no sampling/accurate-estimation modes. HTTP entries and bytes use separate fields and budgets.

## How strict the bound is

Cache hits never wait for eviction. It runs in batches off the read path, so a new entry is stored at once and counted
against `MaxItems` and `WeightLimit` when the next batch applies it. Under any load:

- The counted size or weight is never more than one entry over the bound.
- When writers get ahead of eviction, they wait for it and help with it, so at most `16 × processor count` (at least
  64) inserts, plus two per writing thread, are stored but not yet counted.

Moments after the writes stop, the cache is back within the bound.

## Null values

`null` results are cached by default, so a method that returns `null` isn't run again on every call. Set
`CacheNullValues = false` when `null` means "not there yet" and the next call should try again, or use
[`CacheWhen`](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/conditional-caching.md) for one method.

## Cached objects are shared

> [!WARNING]
> The cache stores the object your method returned and hands the same instance to every caller. Don't change a cached
> object; return immutable types such as records, or copies.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/native-aot.md -->

# Native AOT

MethodCache works in Native AOT and trimmed applications when your cached methods take arguments the decorator can
write into the key itself (see [Keys](#keys) below). The source generator writes the decorators, their registration
and those keys at build time. CI publishes a test application with Native AOT on every change and checks that
caching (with simple, record, collection and `ICacheKeyProvider` arguments), explicit `AutoRegister(ServiceLifetime)` registration and
`[assembly: CacheInterface]` work.

CI also compiles the complete supported signature corpus with Native AOT. This checks generated signatures and
ref safety across all key forms; reflection-based fallback cases retain the runtime limitations described below.

## In-memory caching

Nothing to do: the in-memory cache stores your objects as they are, without serializing them.

## Distributed caching

Values written to Redis, SQL Server or PostgreSQL are serialized with System.Text.Json. Under Native AOT it needs a
`JsonSerializerContext` that lists every type your cached methods return:

```cs
[JsonSerializable(typeof(Product))]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(List<Product>))]   // every type a cached method returns
public sealed partial class ShopJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext;
```

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc
    .UseRedis("localhost:6379")
    .UseJson(ShopJsonContext.Default));
```

Select your context with `MethodCacheBuilder.UseJson(context)`. MethodCache cannot generate this context
for you, because one source generator can't see another generator's output.

## Keys

Under Native AOT, give cached methods arguments that the decorator writes into the key itself:

- simple values (strings, numbers, `bool`, `Guid`, dates, enums),
- records, classes and structs whose public properties and fields are simple values, passed as exactly the declared
  type (a sealed type is safest: an instance of a derived class goes through the key generator),
- types that implement `ICacheKeyProvider`,
- arrays, lists and sets of those (records and classes in them must be sealed), and dictionaries whose keys and values
  are simple values.

Collection subclasses with their own public state also use the key generator; implement `ICacheKeyProvider` on
these types when using Native AOT. Plain lists, arrays and sets keep their inline keys.

Other arguments, such as interfaces, `object` or collections of collections, go through the key generator, which
serializes them with reflection-based System.Text.Json. Publishing then reports trim and AOT warnings (IL2026,
IL3050) from `MethodCache.Core`, and the call throws `InvalidOperationException` at runtime. Wrap such an argument in a type that
implements `ICacheKeyProvider`, as `TenantId` does in [Cache keys](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/keys.md#types-whose-state-is-private).


---

<!-- source: docs/features/testing.md -->

# Testing

The implementation of a cached interface is a plain class: create it directly in unit tests and no caching is
involved.

## Testing with caching

To test the caching itself, such as invalidation tags, build a service provider the way the application does:

```cs
var services = new ServiceCollection();
services.AddSingleton<Database>();
services.AddScoped<IProductService, ProductService>();
services.AddMethodCache();
var provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();

// Resolved through the generated decorator, exactly as in the application
var products = provider.CreateScope().ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IProductService>();
```

`ICacheAdministrator` from the same provider lists the entries and their keys, which helps when a test needs to check
what was cached ([Monitoring](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/monitoring.md)).

## When a test writes to the database directly

A test that changes data without going through a `[CacheInvalidate]` method, such as seeding rows or calling a
repository, leaves the cached results as they were. Clear the cache after the write, or invalidate what it changed:

```cs
await database.SaveAsync(changed);   // the test changes the data behind the cache's back

// Remove everything cached...
await provider.GetRequiredService<ICacheAdministrator>().ClearAsync();

// ...or only what the write changed
var cache = provider.GetRequiredService<ICacheManager>();
```
